books.title: Goodbye, Things
books.author: Fumio Sasaki
needsHumanCheck: The author offers personal experiences and practical suggestions. His results should not be treated as guaranteed outcomes for every reader.
books.hook: Your possessions occupy more than physical space; they also demand attention, care, and decisions.

page1.inOneMinute: Goodbye, Things describes Fumio Sasaki's move toward minimalism and the changes he associates with owning fewer possessions. Sasaki explains how comparison, insecurity, and attachment encouraged him to accumulate things he did not truly need. He then shares practical ways to decide what to keep, reduce clutter, and question the desire to acquire more. Minimalism is presented as a personal choice rather than a competition to own the least. The central idea is that reducing possessions can create room for attention, freedom, and gratitude.
youWillGet: Understand Sasaki's personal approach to minimalism.
Question possessions kept for status or comparison.
Use practical rules to reduce clutter.
Separate personal value from the number of things owned.
page1.whoFor: This book suits readers whose homes feel crowded or whose shopping habits create stress. It is especially useful for people interested in practical decluttering and a simpler relationship with possessions.

glance.mainIdea: Owning fewer unnecessary things can reduce distractions and make daily life easier to manage.
glance.problem: Possessions often accumulate through habit, comparison, and the belief that more things will create happiness.
glance.promise: A deliberate approach to reducing belongings offers more space for attention and meaningful activity.

story.heading: Recognize the weight of possessions
story.text: Sasaki begins with his own experience of stress, dissatisfaction, and comparison with other people. His belongings reflected desires and expectations that did not necessarily improve his daily life. He questions why people acquire objects and why possessions become tied to identity. This reflection sets up minimalism as a change in the relationship with things, not just an exercise in cleaning.

story.heading: Understand why letting go is hard
story.text: The book examines the emotional reasons people keep possessions. Objects may represent past experiences, imagined future needs, or an image of the person someone hopes to become. The effort of deciding what to discard can feel uncomfortable. Sasaki encourages readers to question these attachments and judge objects by their actual place in present life.

story.heading: Reduce belongings in practical ways
story.text: Sasaki provides practical suggestions for reducing possessions and preventing clutter from returning. His methods include examining whether items are used, considering borrowing instead of owning, and keeping photographs of meaningful objects. The purpose is not to follow every rule exactly. It is to develop a more deliberate approach to what enters and remains in the home.

story.heading: Make space for a different life
story.text: The later discussion connects fewer possessions with changes in attention, daily routines, and gratitude. Sasaki describes the personal benefits he associates with minimalism, while presenting his experience as a path readers can consider for themselves. The broader message is that possessions should serve life rather than dominate it. The right amount differs according to needs and circumstances.

author: Fumio Sasaki is a Japanese author, editor, and minimalist. He formerly served as co-editor-in-chief at Wani Books and helped establish the website Minimal & ism. Goodbye, Things draws on his personal experience of reducing his belongings and reconsidering his relationship with possessions. He presents himself as an ordinary person who changed his habits rather than as a professional organizing expert.

Sasaki's writing combines personal reflection with practical advice. He describes the emotional and everyday reasons people keep things, then offers methods for deciding what remains useful. His account connects minimalism with attention, freedom, and gratitude. The book is not a universal rule that everyone should own as little as possible. Its examples invite readers to consider which possessions genuinely serve their lives and which remain through habit or social pressure.
quickFacts: The book's subtitle is The New Japanese Minimalism.
W. W. Norton published the English-language edition.
Sasaki also wrote Hello, Habits: A Minimalist's Guide to a Better Life.

lessons.title: Question why you own it
lessons.text: Sasaki encourages readers to examine the reason behind each possession. Some objects serve a clear purpose, while others remain because of comparison, guilt, or an imagined future. Asking why an item is present makes the decision more deliberate than simply storing it away.
lessons.example: On Sunday afternoon, Riya opens a cupboard and finds exercise equipment she bought after seeing a fitness influencer. She keeps what she uses and lets go of equipment that no longer serves her.

lessons.title: Stop buying for approval
lessons.text: Possessions can become tools for seeking admiration or matching other people's lives. Sasaki's approach questions whether these objects genuinely meet personal needs. Separating private usefulness from social display makes spending and decluttering decisions easier to understand.
lessons.example: After seeing his colleague's expensive watch, Amit wants to buy one too. He waits a week and realizes he values keeping his savings more than owning the same watch.

lessons.title: Use a practical discard rule
lessons.text: Sasaki presents practical rules for deciding what to release, including considering whether an item has been used recently. A rule reduces the need to debate every object from the beginning. The final decision should still reflect genuine needs, accessibility, and the cost of replacing something essential.
lessons.example: While sorting her wardrobe, Neha finds a jacket she has not worn in years. She checks whether it serves a real need before deciding to donate it.

lessons.title: Borrow instead of owning
lessons.text: Some items are needed rarely but occupy space for long periods. Borrowing or sharing can provide access without permanent ownership. This approach is most useful when the item is available reliably and borrowing does not create unreasonable inconvenience for anyone involved.
lessons.example: Kunal needs a drill to assemble a shelf. He borrows one from his neighbour instead of buying a tool he expects to use only once.

lessons.title: Keep memories without every object
lessons.text: Objects can represent meaningful experiences, making disposal feel like losing part of the past. Sasaki suggests that a photograph can preserve the memory without requiring the object to remain. The goal is to keep what matters while questioning whether every physical reminder is necessary.
lessons.example: Maya has boxes of souvenirs from college. She photographs several items, keeps a few favourites, and donates the rest.

lessons.title: Make room for attention
lessons.text: Reducing possessions changes the work involved in cleaning, arranging, and maintaining a home. Sasaki connects a simpler environment with more freedom and gratitude. Minimalism is useful when it supports the life a person wants, rather than becoming another standard for judging oneself.
lessons.example: Every Saturday, Dev spends hours sorting his crowded desk before studying. After removing unused items, he starts his work with fewer distractions and less preparation.

remember: Ask why an item deserves space in your life.
Do not buy things merely to match other people.
Use clear rules to reduce endless decluttering decisions.
Borrow rarely used items when sharing is practical.
A memory does not always require keeping its object.
Minimalism should serve your life, not become another competition.
page4.bigIdea: Owning less is a way to question unnecessary demands on your space, money, and attention.
mistakes: Throwing away useful or necessary belongings simply to reach an arbitrary possession count.
Treating minimalism as a new status symbol or a competition to own less than other people.

exercises.title: Declutter one small area
steps: Remove everything and inspect each item.
Keep what serves a real need or has clear personal value.
Return the useful items and responsibly donate or discard the rest.

exercises.title: Pause before buying
steps: Write down an item you want to purchase.
Identify the need or feeling behind the desire.
Check whether something you already own serves that need.
Decide later whether the purchase still makes sense.

exercises.title: Try borrowing
steps: Identify an item you use only occasionally.
Check whether borrowing or renting is practical.
Compare the cost and convenience with owning it.
Use the better option for your circumstances.

page6.whoShouldRead: Read this book if clutter, shopping, or comparison is making everyday life feel more complicated. It suits readers who want personal reflections alongside practical decluttering suggestions.
page6.whoMightSkip: You may prefer a detailed home-organization manual if you need room-by-room storage instructions. Readers whose possessions are already well suited to their needs may find the main message familiar.

buy.suits: Buy the physical book if you want the full personal story, additional decluttering suggestions, and visual examples.
buy.notSuits: Skip it if this guide gives you enough direction to begin reducing unnecessary possessions.
buy.physicalGives: The complete book offers more personal context, practical methods, and photographs connected with Sasaki's minimalist lifestyle.
